item.title: The Friendship Imbalance No One Talks About
item.description:
Friends

The Friendship Imbalance No One Talks About

What to do when you're carrying the friendship alone.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • A chalant friend is one who reaches out, checks in, and plans hang-outs.
  • New acquaintances are most satisfied in relationships with people who initiate more.
  • Imbalance in effort doesn't always mean imbalance in love—people express care differently.

A chalant friend is one who reaches out, checks in, and plans hang-outs. They’re reliable, intentional, and often a little resentful that their friendships are one-sided.

When I did a speaking event recently, I heard chalant friends express righteous ire. They felt disregarded, taken for granted, and angry at the idea that they had to endlessly give grace to their more passive friends when they had been doing all the work. Some had withdrawn altogether, transforming into nonchalant friends.

To my chalant friends. I see you for the effort you make in friendships. I know you might feel resentful and unloved, but the effort you make is a revolutionary act in a world of loneliness and it means more than you know to the people around you. For example, one study found that new acquaintances are most satisfied in relationships with people who initiate more. It was the single most important factor—more important than disclosure, or social support, for example—that made acquaintances feel more satisfied in the friendship. People love what you do, even if they don’t reciprocate.

But that doesn’t change the resentment and hurt you might feel. If you are feeling that way, here are some of my best tips for working through those feelings:

Mindset Shifts for the Chalant Friend

  1. Discrepancy in intentionality does not mean a discrepancy in love: Once, my friend Zaria (a nonchalant friend) and I (chalant friend) were traveling together, and she had been late for some dinner reservations. We were taking a taxi to the reservation together, so this meant I was late too. I was getting frustrated and feeling disregarded. We talked it out and had a conversation about our general differences around time. Zaria shared that she doesn’t like to feel rushed, especially on vacation, because she really enjoys feeling present in the moment she’s in. That was a breakthrough moment for me. Her being late wasn’t her disrespecting me as much as it was her finding a way to feel more alive, something I want for my friend.
  2. Don’t take it so personally: I know this advice kind of sucks. It sucks to not only feel a bit neglected by others but also to have someone invalidate how bad that feels by telling you that you shouldn’t feel the way that you do. But one thing I’ve learned is that how people treat you is much more about who they are than about who you are. Take a moment to imagine: What if you didn’t perceive your friends’ actions as a reflection of your own worth or value? Then how would you feel?
  3. Recognize love in a different form: Maybe your friend isn’t loving you the way you love them. They don’t text to check in or send you a gift on your birthday. But, they may be a good listener, express appreciation, or you may have great conversations. That matters too. Acknowledge love in different forms.
article continues after advertisement

If those mindset shifts don’t help, you might have to take some actions:

  1. Create friendship structures: If you automatically have a date to hang out on the calendar every month, then no one has to reach out (or feel resentful about it). How can you outsource the planning and logistics? Maybe you and your friends can watch a show together each week, or take a class together.
  2. Voice your needs: The nonchalant friend is often oblivious rather than malicious. They don’t necessarily clock how much effort and intentionality you put into keeping up the friendship—to them, it’s all just happening. You can say to your friend, “I really enjoy spending time with you, but I’m noticing I’m the one reaching out. I’d feel so loved if you’d be open to reaching out more.”
  3. Wait: Perhaps it’s not that your friend will never reach out; it just takes them more time to get around to it. You might want to be in touch monthly, and they want to be in touch quarterly. If you’ve voiced your needs, give them a little more time and see if effort balances out.
  4. Then, stop “taking the L”: Let’s say you tried mindset shifts, you’ve voiced your needs, and nothing has changed. You still feel bitter and resentful. You may be hurt by the imbalance in the friendship, but ultimately resigned, telling yourself, “I’ll just do it; I’ll just reach out,” even if doing it is making you feel resentful. The more resentment you welcome into the friendship, the closer you get to abandoning it altogether. It’s an act of kindness for yourself and your friends for you to stop burning yourself out and disregarding your needs in an asymmetrical friendship.

Your final option is to recalibrate your friendships:

  1. Prioritize friends who meet your needs: I’m not a fan of telling people to give grace when doing so is making them feel neglected and resentful. But one genuine way to increase your capacity to give more grace to others is to get your needs met elsewhere. If you do focus on friends who are as conscientious and engaged as you are, you’ll be a better friend to those who are not.
  2. Find the distance that creates the most intimacy: Maybe if a friend can’t fulfill your need for reciprocity, and that need is really important to you, you can still be friends but at the right level of intimacy. This can be hard, because often when we really like people, we want to be close to them. But (hot take) when deciding who to get close to, prioritize people who fulfill your needs over those who you simply like. You can invest the most time in the friends who invest in you.

And for Nonchalant Friends:

  1. Stop judging yourself. The more you think, “I’m a failure," the more you will disengage.
  2. Deconstruct why you don’t reach out: You’re not burdening or bothering people. You think that if people don’t reach out to you, they don’t want to hear from you. But just as you like it when your friends reach out, perhaps they like it too.
  3. Become more aware of the effort your friends make: Friendships aren’t maintained magically; someone has to be intentional. And if you haven’t been, it’s likely been on your other friends.

item.title: When Cofounders Stop Hearing Each Other, Here's What to Do
item.description:
Coaching

When Cofounders Stop Hearing Each Other, Here's What to Do

Why partnership communication breaks down and what the research suggests.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Stress narrows thinking and speeds up speech.
  • Most cofounder conflict stems from misread behavior.
  • Unresolved tension doesn't disappear between meetings—it accumulates.
  • Pushing a cofounder to change behavior often makes them less likely to change it.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

Two cofounders are in the same meeting room they've been in a hundred times. And, somehow, the conversation feels unproductive. They leave with no action items, no consensus, and when they chat about it next week, they'll have different takeaways.

This is what communication breakdown looks like before it turns into a bigger conflict. And it's more common than most founders want to admit.

This isn't a business problem, it's a relational one. And relationship researchers have useful things to say about it.

The nervous system comes first

When cofounders disagree about something that matters, the conversation often degrades faster than either person expects.

Under stress, the nervous system activates threat-detection responses that narrow thinking, increase emotional reactivity, and reduce listening quality.

Research on stress and prefrontal cortex function shows that acute stress reliably disrupts attentional control and higher-order reasoning—the cognitive resources most needed for nuanced strategic conversation (Liston, McEwen, & Casey, 2009). Speech speeds up, and both individuals start listening to respond instead of listening to truly understand each other's position.

Researcher John Gottman's work on couple communication shows that once this cycle starts, conversations beginning with criticism or contempt rarely end well (Gottman & Levenson, 1992). The same dynamic plays out in business partnerships. The content of the argument almost doesn't matter. The physiological state of the people having it does.

Based on this research, one of the most important interventions is slowing down and regulating your nervous system. When you notice the conversation accelerating—sentences getting clipped, volume creeping up—name it out loud: "I'm feeling activated. Can we slow down?"

This simple intervention works because it shifts both people from reactive to reflective mode before the damage compounds. These micro breaks keep the conversation contained and your nervous system regulated.

The interpretation problem

Here's where most communication advice misses the mark: it focuses on what people say, not on what they assume before they say it.

article continues after advertisement

Cofounders constantly interpret each other's behavior. A missed meeting becomes evidence of disrespect. A quiet day becomes a signal of disengagement. A challenge to an idea becomes a challenge to the person. These feel like observations, but they are presented as accusations and conclusions, and they're often rooted in confirmation bias.

The more useful habit is distinguishing between what you actually observed and the story you're building around it. There's a real difference between "you've seemed distracted the last few times we've talked about growth" and "you're checked out." One opens a door, the other shuts it.

When cofounders default to generous interpretations—assuming positive intent before assuming a negative one—it creates space for deeper dialogue. Gottman's research on long-term partnerships consistently shows that this pattern, what he called "positive sentiment override," is consistently associated with greater relationship stability over time (Gottman & Levenson, 2000).

Emotional residue

Unresolved conflict accumulates and compounds. This emotional debt impacts future conversations because it contributes to greater agitation, assuming negative intent, and defensiveness.

Most cofounder teams don't address this directly. They move on to the next agenda item, assume the last difficult conversation is behind them, and wonder why subsequent conversations feel harder than they should.

article continues after advertisement

The more effective approach is to name the residue when you sense it.

Something like: "I think what happened last month is still impacting me. Would you be open to talking through it so I can feel more resolved and get back to focusing on the future?" This kind of acknowledgment and request tends to defuse a significant portion of the accumulated tension because it breaks the pretense that nothing is lingering. Naming the metaphorical elephant in the room creates relief.

Adding in scheduled relational check-ins—separated from business strategy—serve a similar function. They create a low-stakes container for surfacing tension before it becomes a problem. Consistent small conversations prevent the big ones you didn't see coming.

The control trap

This pattern tends to persist because it often feels justified.

When one cofounder is frustrated with the other's behavior—their decision-making pace, their communication style, their follow-through—the natural instinct is to push for change, directly or indirectly, through feedback or pressure, through restructuring agreements or invoking past commitments. The problem is that this pursuit contributes to defensiveness in the recipient.

Psychologists call the response to this "psychological reactance"—the tendency to push back harder when we feel managed, even when the request itself is reasonable (Brehm, 1966; Miron & Brehm, 2006). The harder you push someone to change a behavior, the more invested they become in maintaining it. This creates a cycle that breeds resentment on both sides and erodes the collaborative dynamic the partnership needs.

"When we delay making these important decisions, it makes me feel anxious that we're not going to be able to capitalize on this opportunity," lands differently than "you're afraid of taking action."

The first is honest about your experience. The second is an interpretation dressed as feedback. Only one of those invites problem-solving.

What to try first

Start with one thing: Slow the next important conversation down by 20–30%. Pause before responding. Notice what happens to your listening quality when you're not already preparing your next point.

From there, here are two questions worth sitting with:

  • When your cofounder's behavior frustrates you, what's the most generous explanation that still fits the facts?
  • Is there a previous conflict between you that hasn't been fully acknowledged—one that might be coloring how you're reading each other right now?
article continues after advertisement

These are calibration questions that can help you to develop enough awareness to interrupt the patterns that are making things harder than they need to be.

item.title: Can the Embodied Self Explain Near-Death Experiences?
item.description:
Near-Death Experiences

Can the Embodied Self Explain Near-Death Experiences?

What disrupted brain-body signals may reveal about selfhood.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • The embodied self model posits that the self is a brain representation of bodily-derived signals.
  • Some pathological conditions and psychedelics disrupt the sense of self that is known as depersonalization.
  • NDE is a conscious experiences include an out-of-body perspective, a light tunnel, and a sense of peace.
  • Could disrupted bodily signals contribute to near-death experiences?

A person's heart stops. Seconds later, consciousness disappears. Yet some people later report floating above their bodies or moving through a tunnel of light. What happens to the self when the body suddenly becomes unavailable to the brain?

Some pioneering scientists, particularly Antonio Damasio and Anil Seth, have proposed that afferent signals from bodily organs and tissues such as the heart, veins, and lungs are represented in the brain as a feeling of self. The function of these signals is mainly to help the brain control and keep the inner bodily environment that called homeostasis. However, the brain, in addition to responding to them to maintain stable homeostasis, represents the sense of self as a byproduct of these signals.

This theory is a fascinating explanation of why we know our body is mine and we agent of our behavior. However, direct evidence for this theory is rare, and therefore, there have been some criticisms of this theory. For instance, it becomes more convincing if we observe that the disruption of these signals in certain pathological conditions impairs the sense of self, resembling a mental state known as depersonalization [1].

What is Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder?

Depersonalization is interesting from a psychological and neuroscientific perspective. It is defined as a persistent or recurrent experience of feeling that one's own thoughts, feelings, body, or actions are strange or unreal to oneself, or one is an outside observer of one's own thoughts, feelings, body, or actions. However, their perception of reality remains intact.

Clinical depersonalization can occur as a symptom in several conditions, such as anxiety and panic disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, major depression, sleep deprivation, neurological disorders, and substance use. It can also manifest as a primary disorder known as depersonalization/derealization disorder, characterized by a chronic experience of unreality. Among drugs that induce depersonalization, cannabis, ketamine, LSD, and psilocybin are commonly associated, most of which are psychedelic substances.

People who use psychedelic drugs often describe a reduced or complete loss of their feeling of being a separate self or ego, distinct from the surrounding world. These compounds act through a specific type of serotonin receptor and change neural circuits. Neuroscientific research into ego dissolution provides valuable insight into the role of the nervous system in self-awareness [2].

Near-Death Experiences (NDEs) and Altered Selfhood

Near-death experiences (NDEs) are a series of profound experiences frequently reported by individuals during life-threatening situations such as cardiac arrest and severe trauma. Despite challenges about NDE in the scientific community, some neuroscientists try to explain them due to their frequent occurrence and the similarity of reports.

article continues after advertisement

Common features of NDEs include a sense of peace, passage through a tunnel, encounters with bright light, and, in some cases, an out-of-body perspective. A less frequently emphasized but potentially important aspect of NDEs is the alteration of the ordinary sense of self. Individuals often report feeling detached from their physical bodies, as if the usual boundaries between self and body have dissolved. These are very similar to the experience of individuals who use psychedelics, therefore someone assumes these hallucinations may arise from natural psychedelics produced by the brain at the end of life [3].

This temporary disruption of embodied selfhood raises an intriguing question: if our sense of self depends on the brain's continuous integration of bodily signals, could NDEs offer a glimpse of what happens when that bodily foundation begins to break down?

Physiological Processes at the End of Life

At the end of life, bodily signals disrupt. After cardiac arrest, blood flow to the brain is almost immediately interrupted. Consciousness is lost within seconds; however, neurons, especially those in the central nervous system, do not die immediately. While the brain's natural inputs are suddenly disrupted, its electrical and metabolic activities continue for a while. The brain tries to maintain the coherence of experience, but the neural network collapses after that [4].

These conditions may be best for investigating the relationship between internal signals and sense of self, if we could trust anecdotes reported by people experienced it. This probable argument for NDE is contradictory with some explanations of NDE, proposed that these experiences are created when brain activity returns and blood circulation is restored.

Competing Explanations for Near-Death Experiences

Most explanations of near-death experiences focus on what happens when the brain is deprived of oxygen, filled with neurochemicals, or begins to recover after circulation returns. But there may be another way to think about these experiences. If our sense of self depends on the brain's continuous integration of signals from the body, then a near-death experience may represent what happens when that bodily foundation suddenly disappears.

article continues after advertisement

Rather than simply producing random hallucinations, the brain may attempt to preserve a coherent sense of self despite losing the internal signals that normally anchor it to the body. In this view, the feeling of leaving the body, moving through a tunnel, or existing as a disembodied observer could reflect a simplified version of the self that emerges when the brain can no longer rely on its usual bodily inputs.

Near-death experiences would therefore not reveal a self-escaping the body, but rather a self-model operating under extreme physiological conditions. If correct, this hypothesis suggests that NDEs may provide a rare opportunity to study how the brain constructs the experience of being a self in the first place.

item.title: Current Mandated Reporter Rules Can Harm Children
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Current Mandated Reporter Rules Can Harm Children

Personal Perspective: We need to empower therapists to use their judgement.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Mandated reporting can drive families out of therapy without improving child safety.
  • Fear of CPS involvement prevents some children from seeking treatment at all.
  • Therapist discretion could focus resources on severe abuse while preserving trust.
A family walks away from therapy towards an uncertain future.
Source: OĞUZHAN YAVUZ / Pexels

“I guess I can’t get therapy then.”

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard something like this from an adolescent client. Having worked in schools, the Medi-Cal (Medicaid) system, and community organizations, I’ve practiced therapy with thousands of children and families. It’s tragic when one-size-fits-all governmental regulations prevent therapy from being successful.

If you don’t know, “mandated reporting” is a legal requirement for therapists and many other professions working with minors, including teachers, physicians, and in California, now even school volunteers. If a mandated reporter becomes aware of child abuse, they are legally obligated to report that abuse to the government.

This mandate is well-intentioned and, on paper, sounds helpful. Why not report abuse and have authorities come in and put a stop to it? Well, not only is that not how it works in practice, but the very existence of the law prevents a lot of children from receiving needed treatment.

Over the years, I’ve had to file dozens of these reports with Child Protective Services (CPS). I’ll start with the practical failures of this policy.

It’s important to consider that there are many forms or corporal punishment that, while in my opinion are still indefensible, are unfortunately very common. For example, a child telling a therapist that a parent slapped them in the face, perhaps even only one time years ago, may still trigger a report and involvement with the system.

We have to bear in mind that CPS and similar agencies in other states are underfunded and overburdened. They have to prioritize the absolute worst cases of abuse to receive the limited available resources. So when a therapist calls up a CPS worker, who is routinely working with situations of children facing unspeakable horrors, and says, “My client told me that they were slapped once 10 years ago”, the worker may be unmoved, or even irritated that valuable staff hours need to be diverted away from higher priority cases to process the report. Even in cases in which I’ve confirmed that I have a legal obligation to report, I’ve actually had CPS workers berate me for wasting their time and say sarcastically, “What do you expect us to do about this?”.

What often happens then is that the family may get a call, or possibly a home visit, from a social worker. Despite the fact that this requirement was explained in the informed consent process, many families still feel betrayed. In my experience, 9 times out of 10, they then immediately withdraw their child from therapy, with trust in therapy irrevocably shattered.

article continues after advertisement

In these cases, the mandated report did not result in the family or child getting any actual resources or support. Instead, it only resulted in the child no longer receiving treatment. In many cases I suspect the relationship between the parent and child is further eroded by the child’s disclosure triggering CPS involvement and may even result in more abuse, which is now completely hidden from the trusted adults in the child’s life. That is a complete failure of the system.

What’s less observable is how many children and families don’t seek treatment in the first place because they know doing so may involve CPS. But sometimes it is possible to actually see this phenomenon play out. I’ve had many instances in which, for example, a teenager comes to treatment and wants to talk about something. I explain my mandated reporting requirements, and they tell me, “Okay, I’m not going to talk to you then.” They leave, untreated, and live with whatever trauma or pain they are carrying for who knows how many years.

So how do we balance the need to provide intervention and help to abused children while still encouraging children and families to participate in treatment?

What I propose for the therapy profession is a reform from mandated reporting to what I might call “discretionary” reporting. If a therapist could use their professional judgement to weigh the risks and benefits of making a report, that would solve a lot of problems. Severe, high priority cases would still frequently get on CPS’s radar and clients would still have trust in the therapeutic process.

Of course, no system is perfect. Even in such a discretionary reporting framework there would be cases in which a therapist did not report a case of severe abuse and an avoidable tragedy later struck. Such an instance might even become a high-profile story in the media. But the issue is that in my opinion, for every one of these, many more tragedies could be avoided if children and families were incentivized to seek out treatment rather than avoid it.

item.title: The Mystery of Alcatraz Continues
item.description:
Forensic Psychology

The Mystery of Alcatraz Continues

Three inmates vanished in the Bay in 1962. The story continues to draw attention.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers vanished from Alcatraz in 1962, the only unsolved escape.
  • A 2013 letter signed by John Anglin claimed all three survived, but the FBI found it inconclusive.
  • U.S. Marshals still keep active warrants, believing the men could be alive in their nineties.
Alcatraz Buildings After 1962 Escape
Source: GGNRA, Park Archives. Public Domain

As President Donald Trump seeks to reopen Alcatraz Federal Penitentiary, the men who pulled off the 1962 escape that made the island legendary vanished, and no one has ever learned what became of them.

Alcatraz was back in the headlines this spring when Trump proposed a fiscal year 2027 budget that asks Congress for $152 million to begin rebuilding the closed-off island prison and eventually reopen it as a federal penitentiary. It's part of a plan he announced in May 2025 to house what he called America's most ruthless and violent offenders.

The news revived the prison's oldest unanswered question: whether anyone escaped Alcatraz alive. Investigators never determined whether the three men drowned in the bay or reached land safely. The case still draws attention, less for the crime than for the unfinished story it left behind.

Why Was Alcatraz Considered Inescapable?

Alcatraz was built to make escape all but impossible. The federal government opened it in 1934 as a penitentiary to hold inmates that other prisons couldn't control. It sits on a rock about a mile and a quarter from the San Francisco shore, surrounded by cold water and strong tidal currents. Back then, guards counted inmates as often as a dozen times a day, plus the cellhouse had steel bars, gun galleries, and watchtowers. For twenty-nine years, thirty-six men attempted fourteen separate escapes. None was ever confirmed to have reached the mainland, let alone survived. The bay was the real barrier.

How the 1962 Alcatraz Escape Was Carried Out

On the night of June 11, 1962, Frank Morris and brothers John and Clarence Anglin broke out. Over several months, they used sharpened spoons to widen the ventilation openings at the backs of their cells. Then they climbed a utility corridor to the roof, went down to the shore, and pushed off on a raft they had made from more than fifty stolen raincoats, along with life vests made the same way. In their beds, they left papier-mâché dummy heads fitted with human hair. A fourth inmate, Allen West, failed to get out of his cell in time and stayed behind. The escape went undetected until the next morning, when a guard reached through the bars, a dummy head fell to the floor, and the prison went into lockdown.

The escape prompted a nationwide manhunt. The FBI, the Coast Guard, the military, and local police joined the search. FBI offices across the country pulled records on the three men and interviewed their relatives. Three convicted bank robbers were at large, and investigators couldn't say where.

The escape's more serious damage was psychological. For nearly thirty years, officials had described Alcatraz as the one prison from which no inmate could escape. Decades later, the question visitors most often ask rangers on the island is whether the men survived.

article continues after advertisement

The public reaction was mixed. Many people admired the audacity of the escape and quietly rooted for the men who pulled it off. The 1979 film Escape from Alcatraz, starring Clint Eastwood as Morris, helped turn the three into folk heroes.

Evidence and Theories Surrounding the Fate of the Escapees

Investigators recovered several items linked to the escape, but never found the men. According to news reports, a paddle and personal belongings were found near Angel Island, with footprints leading away from the shore. Around the same time, a witness told investigators that a blue 1955 Chevrolet had been stolen in nearby Marin County, and a motorist said three men in a blue Chevy had nearly run him off the road. Within a week, shredded rubber believed to be from the raft washed up near the Golden Gate Bridge, and a deflated life jacket surfaced in the water near the island. No bodies, though, surfaced.

The Anglin family later reported a series of contacts. A Christmas card arrived in 1962, signed by John and addressed to their mother. Anonymous flowers reached her every Mother's Day until her death in 1973. The family said two tall men in heavy makeup attended her funeral, and they believed them to be John and Clarence in disguise. In 1975, a family acquaintance produced a photograph said to show the brothers in Brazil. Analysts hired for a later History Channel documentary concluded that the two men in the image closely resembled the Anglins, but the U.S. Marshals Service rejected the theory.


A 2013 Letter Claiming Survival

In 2013, the San Francisco Police Department received a letter from a man claiming to be John Anglin. He said all three had survived the crossing, that Morris had died in 2008 and Clarence in 2011, and that he had cancer and would surrender in exchange for medical care. "Yes we all made it that night but barely!" the letter read. The FBI examined the handwriting, fingerprints, and DNA and found the results inconclusive.

Then, in 2014, a team of Dutch researchers at Delft University of Technology and the Deltares institute used a hydraulic model called 3Di to test the trio's escape against historical tide data. They released dozens of simulated rafts from the island at half-hour intervals. A raft launched just before 11:30 that night would have been carried out through the Golden Gate to the open ocean. A raft that left between 11:30 and midnight could have reached Horseshoe Bay, just north of the bridge. The window for the escapees to survive, they concluded, was about half an hour.

The FBI officially closed its investigation in 1979, concluding that the men had drowned. But the U.S. Marshals Service still lists the case as open, with active arrest warrants for the three men who would now be in their nineties.

Sixty-four years later, the case remains unsolved.

item.title: Musk Gambles, Marx Nods: Economic Abundance Is Not Fulfillment
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Musk Gambles, Marx Nods: Economic Abundance Is Not Fulfillment

A post-scarcity future leaves the most pressing questions unanswered.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Elon Musk’s capitalist vision of absolute abundance ironically mirrors Karl Marx’s socialist dream.
  • Endless material abundance raises knotty questions about wealth distribution and finite planetary limits.
  • Humans require psychological friction to thrive; comfort without struggle may cause existential atrophy.

Aside from their belief in free trade, few convictions are more universally held among economists than the idea that there will always be ample jobs for all. The standard view holds that while new technologies inevitably produce short-term dislocations—creating winners and losers, punishing those slow to adapt—in the long run, heightened productivity fuels broader growth and prosperity.

This optimism is so ingrained that, when a colleague and I surveyed economics professors across the U.S. about a decade ago, only around 7% considered mass structural unemployment a realistic prospect in the coming decades. The main dissenters? A small subset of radical, Marxist-leaning economists, among whom roughly 40% viewed such a scenario as plausible.

How the Rise of AI Has Shifted Economic and Social Anxiety

That survey predated the explosive rise of A.I. Back then, warnings about technology-driven job obsolescence felt more theoretical than imminent. Today, the conversation has shifted dramatically: discussions of universal basic income (UBI) as a necessary buffer against widespread displacement are no longer fringe. The idea has even featured as a core plank in a former presidential candidate's platform, reflecting how quickly public anxiety about automation has moved from the margins to the mainstream.

Musk Gambles, Marx Nods: A Post-Scarcity Vision Parallels Marxist Utopianism

One figure who does not share in the collective anxiety over automation is Elon Musk. Now the world’s first trillionaire techno-optimist, Musk has professed all manner of utopian forecasts in his posts and talks:

  • “AI and robots are going to make so much stuff and provide so many services that they’ll run out of things to do for humans.”
    (Abundance Summit, June 11, 2026)
  • “The robots will actually make so many robots and A.I. that they will actually saturate all human needs.”
    (World Economic Forum, Davos, Switzerland, January 22, 2026)
  • "I think long term, money disappears as a concept. In a future where anyone can have anything, I think you no longer need money as a database for labor allocation. If AI and robotics are big enough to satisfy all human needs, then money will lose its relevance."
    (WTF Podcast, November 30, 2025)
Source: ChatGPT AI image/Free use

The irony of Musk’s speculations is that they envision a world quite congruent with the loftiest dreams of democratic socialists. Of course, it would be absurd to presume that the world’s richest capitalist now shares Karl Marx’s worldview. Yet his speculations are wholly consistent with the famous communist’s most utopian aims. Marx approvingly quotes Aristotle in the Politics that if the “creations of Daedalus moved of themselves,” or if the “weavers’ shuttles were to weave of themselves,” then there would be no need of “masters,” “slaves” or “apprentices.”

article continues after advertisement

As captivating as such speculations seem, I suggest that they fail to address the most pressing questions facing human beings.

Key Barriers to a Post-Scarcity Future

Who gets to share in the abundance? If AI and robots perform most productive labor, how will people obtain the purchasing power needed to consume the goods and services produced? Or, if money is phased out entirely, on what principle will people gain access to goods, including scarce ones like beachfront homes? Elon Musk has hardly addressed these deeper distributional questions. Any solution — whether universal basic income, some other redistributive mechanism, or the kind of central planning favored by democratic socialists — would likely ignite fierce political conflict over access, fairness, and economic priorities.

Can abundance coexist with ecological limits? Human desires may be unlimited, but the Earth's resources are not. Any vision of human flourishing built upon ever-expanding consumption collides with ecological reality. The World Wildlife Fund's 2024 Living Planet Report notes a staggering 73 percent loss in monitored wildlife since 1970, due to habitat destruction, overexploitation, and climate change. If technological progress simply enables humanity to consume ever more goods and energy, rather than helping us live more sustainably, then Musk's vision of abundance is not a solution to our ecological predicament—it is an intensification of it.

Can people thrive without purpose? Even if the economic and ecological challenges could somehow be resolved, a deeper psychological question remains. Human beings need more than comfort, entertainment, and material security. As the psychiatrist Viktor Frankl observed, human thriving does not come from a state of tensionless comfort, but from the productive tension between a person and a difficult goal. People derive meaning from pursuing goals, overcoming obstacles, and contributing to something larger than themselves. Throughout most of human history, survival demanded effort, responsibility, and cooperation. A world in which machines satisfy our every need may free us from necessity, but it may also deprive us of many of the struggles through which character, competence, and purpose are formed. As the 2008 film Wall-E warns, a life without constraint can drift toward passivity, distraction, and sloth. The risk is not simply laziness in a moral sense, but a gradual atrophy of the capacities that make sustained effort meaningful in the first place.

Source: Gemini AI image/Free use

Ultimately, both Musk’s capitalist gamble and Marx’s socialist dream share a common blind spot: they treat material scarcity as humanity’s central problem. Psychology suggests otherwise. Solving the problem of survival does not automatically solve the problem of meaning. If technology strips away the demands of daily life, we must intentionally construct new frameworks for purpose, effort, community, and self-sacrifice. A post-scarcity society may not fail because it lacks resources, but because it lacks a blueprint for human flourishing.

item.title: What the World Cup Can Teach Us About Cultural Humility
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

What the World Cup Can Teach Us About Cultural Humility

How soccer's biggest stage challenges assumptions about identity and belonging.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • The World Cup reveals how ideas about identity and belonging are changing globally.
  • Many viewers are seeing national teams that challenge old assumptions about culture.
  • Cultural humility begins when we question our surprise instead of defending it.
  • Curiosity about differences can strengthen empathy, connection, and respect.

As a longtime soccer fan, one of my favorite parts of the World Cup has little to do with goals, standings, or championship predictions.

I enjoy watching the world show up on one field and encounter itself.

Recently, I was talking with family members who had watched some of the World Cup matches. They commented on the number of Black and Brown players representing countries they had always imagined as racially homogeneous.

One remarked, “I didn’t realize there were so many Black players on that team.”

Another wondered aloud whether some of the players were actually from the countries they represented.

The comments were not hostile. They reflected genuine surprise.

What struck me was that I was surprised by their surprise.

As a long-time soccer fan who has followed international soccer for years, I have become accustomed to seeing multicultural teams. Many international leagues have long reflected the realities of migration, globalization, and multicultural societies. For many American viewers who only tune in during the World Cup, however, these changes can appear sudden.

Yet what we are witnessing on the world’s biggest sporting stage is not simply a shift in soccer. It is a shift in how we understand identity, nationality, and belonging.

More importantly, it is an opportunity to practice cultural humility.

The concept of cultural humility was introduced by physicians Melanie Tervalon and Jann Murray-García (1998) as an alternative to the idea of cultural competence. Rather than assuming we can become “competent” in another person’s culture, cultural humility emphasizes lifelong learning, self-reflection, openness, and a willingness to recognize the limits of our own perspectives.

In other words, cultural humility asks us to approach difference with curiosity rather than certainty.

The World Cup provides a surprisingly powerful setting for this kind of learning.

Many of us carry unconscious assumptions about what different nations “look like.” We develop mental images based on history books, media portrayals, family stories, stereotypes, travel experiences, or what we were taught growing up. We may assume that a country has one dominant racial, ethnic, or cultural identity. We may unconsciously equate nationality with appearance, accent, ancestry, or skin color.

article continues after advertisement

Then the World Cup begins.

The English Premier League, Germany's Bundesliga, Spain's La Liga, France's Ligue 1, and other major leagues have long reflected the realities of migration, globalization, and multicultural societies.
Source: Md Jawadur Rahman / Pexels

We see athletes whose identities complicate those assumptions. We see players who are children of immigrants, members of diaspora communities, or people with cultural roots that span more than one nation. We see teams that reflect migration, colonial history, interracial families, and global movement.

For some viewers, this creates cognitive dissonance—a psychological experience that occurs when new information challenges existing beliefs. That discomfort can become a doorway to growth.

The goal of cultural humility is not to eliminate surprise. It is to become curious about it.

Instead of asking, “Why are there so many Black players on that team?” cultural humility invites us to ask, “What assumptions was I carrying about this country in the first place?”

That subtle shift changes everything.

The World Cup reminds us that identity is far more complex than many of us were taught to believe. A player can represent a nation fully and still carry family history from somewhere else. A person can belong to more than one cultural story. A national team can reflect both tradition and transformation.

As a BIPOC soccer fan, one of the most meaningful aspects of recent tournaments has been seeing how representation has expanded across the global game. Growing up, it was common to see certain countries represented through narrow cultural images. Today, many teams reflect a wider range of racial, ethnic, and cultural backgrounds.

This visibility matters.

Psychologists have long recognized that representation influences our understanding of who belongs in particular spaces. Social identity theory suggests that people develop a sense of self partly through group membership and social categorization (Tajfel & Turner, 1979). The people we see occupying valued roles help shape our perceptions of possibility, legitimacy, and belonging.

article continues after advertisement

When children watch the World Cup and see athletes who look like them representing nations around the world, their understanding of belonging expands.

But cultural humility requires more than noticing diversity.

It asks us to reflect on our own reactions.

One way to practice cultural humility is to pause when we feel surprised by someone’s identity. Surprise is information. It tells us that we were carrying an expectation, even if we did not realize it. Instead of judging ourselves harshly or becoming defensive, we can ask: What did I assume? Where did that assumption come from? What else might I need to learn?

Another way to practice cultural humility is to resist making one person responsible for explaining an entire group. A single player, colleague, student, client, or neighbor cannot represent a whole culture. Cultural humility allows us to appreciate someone’s background without reducing them to it.

We can also practice cultural humility by listening more carefully to how people describe themselves. Identity is not only assigned from the outside. It is lived from the inside. The labels that matter most are often the ones people choose for themselves.

The benefits of cultural humility extend far beyond soccer.

Cultural humility can improve relationships because it helps us listen without rushing to categorize people. It can reduce stereotyping because it interrupts the assumption that we already know who someone is. It can support empathy because it encourages us to ask better questions. It can also help create safer schools, workplaces, therapy spaces, and communities because people are less likely to feel flattened, exoticized, or misunderstood.

In clinical and helping professions, cultural humility has been associated with stronger therapeutic relationships and more respectful cross-cultural care (Hook et al., 2013). But the concept is useful for everyone because all of us live in a world shaped by difference.

The modern world is increasingly shaped by migration, dual citizenship, mixed-race families, global mobility, and layered identities. The World Cup simply makes these realities visible.

article continues after advertisement

There are still countries whose teams appear relatively homogeneous. There are still social tensions surrounding race, citizenship, immigration, and national identity. There are still painful debates about who is accepted, who is questioned, and who has to prove belonging.

The World Cup does not erase those realities.

What it does offer is a unique opportunity to observe them.

For one month, billions of people watch athletes represent nations in ways that challenge conventional ideas about culture, race, and identity. Every match becomes an invitation to reconsider what we think we know about other people.

Beyond the trophies, rivalries, and spectacle, the World Cup teaches us that identity is more complex than stereotypes, belonging is broader than appearances, and understanding begins with curiosity.

That is the heart of cultural humility.

And it may be one of the most valuable lessons the tournament has to offer.

item.title: Chemistry Isn’t Magnetic. It’s Neuroscience
item.description:
Neuroscience

Chemistry Isn’t Magnetic. It’s Neuroscience

The surprising science to make people feel instantly connected to you.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Chemistry is less about fate and more about how the brain builds connection.
  • Small communication strategies can make others feel more seen, valued, and connected.
  • Hope grows when we stop waiting for connection and start creating it.

Just about everyone has heard someone say, “We have chemistry,” as if they have some magic force that is invisible and unexplainable between them.

However, human neuroscience tells another story: It appears that what we refer to as “chemistry” actually occurs in terms of how the brain processes those first few minutes of any interaction. The words that you use, the questions that you ask, and the way you respond to other people all have tremendous power to shape how that person feels about you.

Here are three neuroscience-backed ways to build chemistry with anyone you meet.

1. Give Their Brain a Positive Emotional Experience

The worst way to start a conversation where you want to boost chemistry is by asking the typical question, “How are you?”

The problem with “How are you?” is that it will ultimately produce a very predictable answer, and after that, the person you are talking to will lose interest in talking to you.

Instead of asking a question that produces a predictable response, i.e., “How are you?” use a question that makes someone think back to a positive memory about themselves, such as;

  • What made you smile today?

  • What are you looking forward to this week?

  • What would you say has been the best experience of the month so far?

According to research, recalling a positive memory can actually re-establish the positive feelings associated with that memory, which temporarily increases overall positive feelings (Joormann & Siemer, 2004). In addition to feeling an increased sense of "positive emotion," you also become associated with this positive feeling, boosting your overall connection. Chemistry is not created out of thin air! This approach helps your first experience with another person be a positive one, so they walk away feeling good about you and the interaction.

2. Keep the Conversation Rewarding With Dopamine Hits

One of the brain's major reward systems — our mesolimbic dopamine pathway — will respond to potential rewards we are about to receive (Berridge & Robinson, 2016) and urge us to pursue them.

To make a rewarding conversational exchange, you should have curiosity for that person first. When someone tells you a story, like what happened on that trip, as an example, instead of answering the person immediately with your story about your trip, ask them another question: What happened after that? Michael, why did you choose to do that?

article continues after advertisement

Include the person's name in your follow-up questions. Your name is one of the most meaningful things to you because it captures your attention, activates the areas of your brain that process the self, and causes the brain to release dopamine, a reward chemical (Carmody & Lewis, 2006).

When combined with some follow-up questions, using the person's name will show him or her that you find them interesting and make them want to keep talking. Charismatic speakers often get the credit for being good speakers, but they are truly great listeners who make others feel appreciated and special.

3. Mirroring for Rapport

Have you met someone and didn't know why you felt comfortable around him or her? Your body was silently communicating with theirs.

The "chameleon effect" has been documented by psychologists: Our innate ability to subconsciously mimic or mirror each other's body postures, gestures, facial expressions, or the way a person speaks to us creates a sense of likeness and mutual rapport (Chartrand & Bargh, 1999).

Subtlety is key — when you abruptly copy someone's body movements, it feels forced and, in my humble opinion, disingenuous. Instead, over the duration of a conversation, be mindful of your body language so it gradually blends in with theirs. If they lean in, you lean in. If they speak slowly, then you should speak slowly. Smile back if they smile.

The point is to attune your body language to each person. You will be able to develop a more meaningful connection with him or her by making the other person feel safe and secure when they are around you.

Hope Grows with Connection

Chemistry does not have to be mysterious, and it's not something you have or you don't.

Hope teaches us to believe that we have the ability to achieve meaningful goals because there is a path to achieve them (Snyder 2002). So, if connection can be developed intentionally, then every conversation provides us with an opportunity to create relationships, create community, and find hope together.

article continues after advertisement

Creating a positive experience for someone else, having a real conversation with them so they feel they are "being heard," and fostering a sense of psychological safety are what happen when you create the conditions for connection.

Chemistry is not just a matter of being "magnetic" with someone. It's all about neuroscience.

Hope is built when we take action to create connections with others as opposed to waiting for the connection to occur. Each and every conversation provides a chance for us to give the other person a sense of being seen, appreciated/valued, and understood. And at times, this is all that chemistry is.
